articles.title: Israel elections: Netanyahu faces crucial test; reports of fraud attempts, missing ballots - top developments
articles.summary: Israelis are voting in a crucial parliamentary election on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a major test of his leadership amid
articles.body: Israelis are voting in a crucial parliamentary election on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a major test of his leadership amid unresolved conflicts, divisions over the country's future and growing international criticism of its conduct in Gaza.Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to retain power against a group of parties hoping to unseat him, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.The election is the country's first national vote since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack that triggered the war in Gaza and related regional conflicts.However, reports of missing, damaged and defaced ballot slips have raised concerns about election integrity, with Eisenkot's Yashar party filing a complaint with the Central Elections Committee.1. Netanyahu faces a crucial testThe election is a test not only of Netanyahu's leadership but also of the direction Israel should take, with voters divided over security, military conscription, judicial independence and the country's international standing.Netanyahu's supporters view him as an experienced leader who has guided Israel through multiple wars and defended its Jewish identity.His critics accuse him of prolonging the war in Gaza and the hostage crisis for political reasons, undermining judicial independence and allowing ultra-Orthodox religious men to avoid compulsory military service.“The present government is driving the country into the ground,” voter Angela Bengur said in Jerusalem, the Associated Press reported.Eisenkot's supporters see him as a leader with strong security credentials who could improve Israel's international standing and strengthen democratic institutions. His personal losses during the Gaza war have also shaped his public image: his son and two nephews were killed while fighting in Gaza.2. Voter turnout hits highest midday level since 1973Voter turnout in Israel’s parliamentary election reached 31.5% by noon local time, the highest recorded at that hour since 1973, according to The Times of Israel, citing the Central Elections Committee.The strong participation reflects intense voter engagement as Israelis cast their ballots at more than 12,000 polling stations across the country.Turnout had already reached 16.68% by 10 am, with more than one million people having voted, the Central Elections Committee said. The figure was higher than the 15.9% recorded at the same time during the 2022 election.The Times of Israel reported that the morning turnout was the highest at that hour since at least 1996, when Benjamin Netanyahu first became prime minister. Other reports described it as the highest since 1981.Around 330,000 young Israelis are eligible to vote for the first time. Many are approaching compulsory military service as the country continues to grapple with the consequences of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and the wars that followed.Turnout among Israel Defense Forces (IDF) personnel was also higher than in the previous election. The IDF said 30% of service members had voted by 10 am, compared with 25.7% at the same point in 2022.3. Netanyahu warns of Arab-backed govt as Arab-led parties eye key roleArab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers in Israel’s parliamentary election if rival political blocs fail to secure a majority, potentially playing a decisive role in government formation, according to AP reports.Netanyahu urged Likud supporters to turn out in large numbers, warning that the country’s future was at stake.“This is an emergency call to Likud voters! Today no one stays home. No sea, no barbecue. Making sure that the family, friends, and neighbors also get to the polling station,” he wrote on X, sharing a video.“The future of our Jewish state is on the line: a strong right-wing government or a left-wing government supported by the Arab parties. Going out to vote with all our might!” he added.In another post, Netanyahu said buses were heading to polling stations and long queues were being reported in Arab communities, while right-wing strongholds had yet to see a comparable turnout.“If we don't go out to vote now, we'll find ourselves with a government of the Arab parties. We must not stay home. Every vote counts! Going out now to vote - Machal, Likud,” he wrote.Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population, giving Arab-led parties the potential to influence government formation if the main political blocs fall short of a majority.“Our vote will change the government,” Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra’am party, said after casting his vote. He added that he hoped turnout in Arab communities would exceed 70%.However, cooperation with Arab-led parties remains a contentious issue among right-wing politicians.Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has faced criticism for his treatment of Palestinian detainees and remarks about Palestinians in Gaza, warned that “it will be Mansour Abbas’ government” if Netanyahu and his allies fail to secure a victory.4. Yashar party alleges ballot tampering, files complaintEisenkot's Yashar party has filed a complaint with the Central Elections Committee over reports that ballot slips bearing its designated voting symbol, “Derech”, were missing, damaged or defaced at polling stations.The party said it had received reports from several locations across the country about ballot slips being removed, marked with pens or turned over inside voting booths, potentially resulting in votes being disqualified.“After Likud's fake news campaign, we received numerous complaints about our ballot slips being defaced or removed,” party chairman Yoaz Hendel said, The Jerusalem Post reported.The party described the alleged incidents as a possible systematic attempt to disrupt its vote and undermine election integrity.“Anyone who tries to steal ballot slips is trying to steal the election. This is a serious violation of election integrity and the fundamental right of Israeli citizens to vote,” the party said.The allegations had not been independently established in the information available at the time of reporting.5. Eisenkot visits October 7-hit community before votingEisenkot began election day by visiting Kibbutz Nir Oz, one of the communities hardest hit by the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack.He walked alongside former hostage Gadi Mozes towards his polling booth before leaving to cast his own vote elsewhere.“I am proud and moved to begin this day with Gadi Mozes, a symbol of the Israeli spirit and strength, of Israelis’ commitment to one another and their commitment to the state. I pledge to do everything I can to ensure that we are worthy of the price you paid, the price the kibbutz paid and the price we all paid, and to bring healing and repair to all citizens of Israel,” Eisenkot told reporters.Mozes endured 482 days in Hamas captivity and campaigned for Eisenkot, according to The Times of Israel.Eisenkot also criticised the government for not beginning election day in communities attacked on October 7. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here in the Gaza envelope,” he said.Netanyahu had not appeared in public in the first three hours after polling stations opened, according to the initial reports. In Tel Aviv, families of people killed during the October 7 attack and former hostages observed a moment of silence.6. President Herzog calls election a 'holiday of democracy'President Isaac Herzog visited the Central Elections Committee headquarters and urged Israelis to participate in the democratic process.“It is a real holiday of democracy, and no one can be allowed to ruin it — quite the opposite, this is our opportunity, all of us, to influence our fate, the fate of our children, and the fate of our grandchildren. It is something that is deeply embedded inside of our spirit, as a very democratic nation,” The Times of Israel reported him as saying.“We are putting different slips in the ballot, and we are expressing different opinions, in the end we have a common fate. A common fate in this land, a common fate in our beloved country, and this election process is another way to express our love for our country,” Herzog added.7. Israel deploys 100,000 personnel for election dayIsrael has mounted a large logistical operation for the parliamentary election, with around 100,000 personnel, including election officials and workers, deployed across the country.Acting director general of the Central Elections Committee Dean Livne said around 50,000 election workers had received training at approximately 2,140 venues.The committee has prepared 12,018 polling stations, 18,000 ballot boxes, 12 million voting envelopes and 250 tonnes of paper for ballot materials. It has also established 6,209 accessible polling stations.Special voting arrangements have been made for more than 600,000 people who may be unable to vote at their designated polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats and hospitalised voters. These voters can use an outer-envelope system, with checks designed to prevent duplicate voting.Authorities have also arranged free travel on 660 intercity public transport routes, including all Israel Railways services, to help voters reach polling stations. Around 690 million shekels, or approximately $223 million, has been allocated for the election.The Central Elections Committee has deployed around 15,000 cameras for electoral integrity inspectors to monitor polling stations and document voting and counting. The system is intended to protect ballot secrecy and allow inspectors to identify attempts to pressure or influence voters.8. How Israel's electoral system worksIsrael is a parliamentary democracy in which voters elect lawmakers rather than directly choosing the prime minister. The government must retain the confidence of the Knesset to remain in power.The country uses a proportional representation system. Voters choose a party list, and the 120 seats in the Knesset are distributed broadly in proportion to the votes received by parties that cross the electoral threshold.Unlike many other parliamentary democracies, Israel treats the entire country as a single constituency rather than dividing it into geographic electoral districts. This allows smaller parties representing religious, political and ethnic communities to win parliamentary representation.Parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter the Knesset. The system often produces fragmented parliaments in which no single party wins an outright majority, making coalition negotiations central to government formation.9. What happens after the votes are counted?After the results are finalised, President Herzog will consult the leaders of the elected parties before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.The person chosen does not necessarily have to lead the largest party; the key consideration is who appears most likely to assemble a coalition with sufficient parliamentary support.The designated lawmaker will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. If the attempt fails, another party leader may be given 28 days to try.If that effort also fails, at least 61 lawmakers can request that the president assign the task to a particular member of the Knesset within a further 21-day period.A new government must win a confidence vote in parliament. A minority government may also take office if it receives more votes in favour than against, even without the backing of 61 lawmakers.The process could take weeks, leaving the identity of Israel's next prime minister uncertain even after election results emerge. If all attempts to form a government fail, the country could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a new government takes office.10. Iran tensions remain in the backgroundThe election is also taking place amid continuing tensions with Iran. Netanyahu intensified his warnings to Tehran ahead of the vote, saying it would face “a devastating blow” if it attacked Israel.Israel's conduct in Gaza and the occupied West Bank has also drawn growing international criticism. Public support for Israel in the US has fallen, while some European and other partners have imposed sanctions.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Built in 1906, a San Francisco mansion later served as a theatre, reportedly a brothel and a wartime officers' club; after restoration, the 9,545-square-foot Verdier Mansion is now listed for $25 million
articles.summary: A historic mansion in San Francisco’s Russian Hill neighbourhood, once associated with a wealthy businessman’s romantic scandal and later linked to an
articles.body: A historic mansion in San Francisco’s Russian Hill neighbourhood, once associated with a wealthy businessman’s romantic scandal and later linked to an opium den, a theatre, a reported brothel and a World War II officers’ club, has returned to the property market with an asking price of $25 million. Known as the Verdier Mansion, the six-level residence at 1001 Vallejo Street spans 9,545 square feet and is being offered for sale after two decades under its current owners.According to SFGATE, the mansion was designed in 1906 by architect Houghton Sawyer for Robert G. Hanford, a businessman who made his fortune through mining and railways. The property’s current listing on confirms the $25 million asking price and the home’s 9,545-square-foot area. However, real-estate databases list 1907 as its construction year, while historic-district records date the mansion to 1905-1906.A mansion built around a controversial romanceThe house was commissioned by Hanford for Gabrielle Guittard Cavalsky, a member of the family behind Guittard Chocolate. A 2006 historical feature by SFGATE, drawing on research by an earlier listing agent, recounted the couple’s relationship as a dramatic romance involving two married people. Hanford reportedly described his feelings for Cavalsky as a once-in-a-lifetime passion in a letter to his wife. The relationship eventually ended in divorce, but the mansion remained a reminder of the affair. Its grand living room, which was designed to accommodate musical performances, reportedly hosted gatherings where Cavalsky sang while musicians accompanied her.The property changed hands over the following years. In 1919, it was purchased by Paul Verdier, associated with San Francisco’s City of Paris department store, and the residence subsequently became known as the Verdier Mansion. The National Park Service’s historic-district nomination identifies the building as the Hanford-Verdier Mansion and credits Sawyer as its architect.From artists’ gatherings to a reported brothelThe mansion’s later history was considerably less conventional than its beginnings as a private residence. According to SFGATE’s historical account, the property passed through periods of neglect and changing use after the Verdier family moved out. The building reportedly became an opium den after squatters entered it. Its ballroom also hosted artists’ gatherings, including events described as Artists Balls, while an earlier period saw the house used as a bohemian meeting place for literary and artistic circles.One of its most notorious reported associations was with Sally Stanford, a well-known San Francisco madam. Historical accounts cited by SFGATE describe the mansion as having been used for prostitution, drinking and gambling during Stanford’s time there. These accounts form part of the property’s reported history rather than a complete, independently documented record of every use of the building.During World War II, the mansion reportedly served as an officers’ club, where military personnel could socialise and be entertained. The SFGATE feature also said that John F. Kennedy was believed to have visited the property 17 times. That detail remains a reported historical claim and should not be treated as independently established fact.The mansion later went through further ownership changes. In the early 1950s, it was sold at auction to Catherine Doliani, who was reported to have divided the building into apartments. Its changing uses reflected a period when the grand residence was no longer functioning solely as the private home for which it had been designed.Restoration returned the mansion to its former grandeurThe property underwent a major restoration in 1992, when physician Thomas Grotz and his wife, Lena, worked to restore its grandeur and update its interiors. The earlier SFGATE report described additions including a spiral staircase, a modern kitchen and luxury finishes.Economist Myron Scholes, who received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1997, later owned the mansion. He and his wife, Jan Blaustein, bought it in 1998, according to the historical report. The property was subsequently purchased by John and Donna Skeen in 2006 for $12 million. The current listing marks its return to the market after 20 years with the couple.Six levels, gardens and sweeping city viewsThe current listing describes the mansion as a six-bedroom residence spread across six levels, with six full bathrooms and two powder rooms. It occupies an approximately 8,285-square-foot lot near the Vallejo Street steps in Russian Hill, an established San Francisco neighbourhood known for its steep streets and city views.The home includes an elevator connecting its floors, a temperature-controlled wine cellar, gardens, terraces and an interior courtyard. Its principal rooms feature period woodwork and detailed finishes, while the property’s elevated position offers views of the city skyline and landmarks including the Bay Bridge and Coit Tower.A long garage that can accommodate five or six vehicles is another notable feature of the property, according to the listing. The combination of historic architecture, extensive interior space and outdoor areas makes the mansion unusual in a city where large private homes are relatively scarce.The $25 million asking price places the Verdier Mansion among San Francisco’s high-end residential listings. Whether it sells at that price remains to be seen, but its appeal rests on more than its size and location: the house carries a century-long history that moves from a wealthy businessman’s romantic scandal to artists’ gatherings, reported illicit activity, wartime use and a modern restoration.For a prospective buyer, the property offers a restored historic residence. For San Francisco, it remains a reminder of how a single building can reflect the changing social life of a neighbourhood across generations.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court
articles.summary: News organisations are challenging the law, arguing it could hamper investigative journalism and endanger sources.
articles.body:
The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounts to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups have told the Supreme Court.

A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s law on Tuesday, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow the government to identify journalists’ sources, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), told judges.

“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission … it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”

The Supreme Court said it would hear the case next month.

Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written exemption for journalists as in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.

The DNPA’s members include Ambani’s Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani’s NDTV and other high-profile media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.

A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, says the group’s filing, cited by the Reuters news agency.

A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent “would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses”.

The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which the DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report.

News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for noncompliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the “interests of the general public”, which would curtail press freedom, the DNPA said.

From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organisation handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said.

It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued.

The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

articles.title: Wall blown over by Storm Boelo in Whitby sparks AI images debate
articles.summary: Vehicles were damaged near Whitby Abbey, but dozens of online comments claimed the photos were fake.
articles.body:
The collapse of a stone wall in an historical churchyard may not be the most likely reason to discuss artificial intelligence (AI).

The battle over the regulation of the technology, copyright law, use of data centres and more are frequently in the spotlight just now.

But the question of AI-generated images is one that refuses to go away - and during Storm Boelo, that question reared its head again.

As the storm abated in the North Yorkshire coastal resort town of Whitby, publican Sue Taylor was out for a stroll.

She snapped images of rocks from a collapsed wall, close to the town's famed abbey, sitting neatly on the bonnets of adjacent cars and shared the pictures online.

The 48-year-old, who runs the Black Horse Pub in the town, said she saw the damage while on her normal dog-walking route.

"It was a shocker," she said, adding that the permit-only parking spaces were used by people living nearby or at the side of the landmark 199 Steps route up to the abbey.

"I used to live up near the abbey for about 12 and a half years, and although we experienced some strong winds, I'd never seen it be strong enough for a wall to be blown over during the night."

Taylor said she took two photographs and posted them on Facebook when she got back to her office, without any editing.

Dozens of comments on the post said the images were created or changed using AI.

"It's not something that I would ever have considered altering, let alone know where to start," Taylor explained.

She described the online doubt from internet sleuths as "a bit ridiculous".

The BBC has viewed independently-posted photographs and videos of the same damage online and spoken to eyewitnesses who corroborated Taylor's images.

Prof Theocharis Kyriacou, an expert on AI at York St John University, said he could understand some viewers' scepticism, but urged caution, particularly as "real people" had been affected by the incident.

"Some of the rocks appear to have fallen into rather neat or unusual arrangements, which might seem surprising," he added.

"However, we should remember that most of us have probably never witnessed this particular type of structural collapse before.

"Something looking unusual or unexpected does not necessarily make it artificial."

Photos from different sources, independent footage and eyewitness accounts were "more meaningful than individual impressions of what looks real or fake", Kyriacou explained.

He said the photographs from Whitby illustrated a "wider issue" as trust in visual evidence was "eroded".

"For generations, photographs have been regarded as relatively reliable representations of reality," he said.

"Now, because of the misuse of generative AI, even genuine photographs, are increasingly being questioned. That is a rather sad consequence of what is otherwise a remarkable technological achievement."

North Yorkshire may be seen by some who live there, and many visitors, as a bastion of the past.

It boasts Victorian seaside towns like Whitby, a slew of high-profile monastic ruins, such as Rievaulx Abbey and Bolton Abbey, and the famous Roman walls and medieval buildings of York itself.

But the area, like everywhere else, is faced with challenges around understanding what is real and what is not as technology races ahead.

Earlier this year, a senior York politician was targeted by AI-generated deepfake images and received police advice to step up security at his home.

The fake video appeared to show Pete Kilbane, the city council's Labour deputy leader, handing cash to men in balaclavas. An unspecified flag then appeared behind him.

Kilbane said he was "shocked" when he first saw the video, adding: "This is an attempt to undermine democracy and make legitimate, factual debate impossible."

Last month, university students raised concerns over the software used to submit assignments and check them for plagiarism, amid fears their work could be used to train tools which use AI.

The University of York Students' Union said planned changes to the licence agreement for the Turnitin system could see students' work used to teach AI models.

The university said it would review any changes to the software's terms and conditions.

A spokesperson for Turnitin said its policy would not be updated any earlier than September 2027 to "give us time to discuss any changes with customers".

Kyriacou said AI-generated images and video posted during deadly floods in Nepal were a "particularly troubling example" of the technology being misused.

He encouraged people to "question what they encounter online rather than accept everything at face value".

"But there is an important distinction between healthy scepticism and automatically dismissing something as fake simply because it looks extraordinary."

A spokesperson for English Heritage, which operates Whitby Abbey, said the incident involving the wall had not impacted its operations.

A Whitby Abbey Illuminated event was separately cancelled because of the weather over the weekend but resumed on Monday evening, they added.

The BBC has contacted The Parish of Whitby and Ruswarp, which is responsible for St Mary's Church, and North Yorkshire Council for a comment.

articles.title: A proposal is more about power than love. Rashmika Mandanna proposing to Vijay Deverakonda 100 times doesn’t make her a doormat.
articles.summary: India has lost its mind because Rashmika Mandanna proposed to Vijay Deverakonda “100 times”.
articles.body: India has lost its mind because Rashmika Mandanna proposed to Vijay Deverakonda “100 times”. Now, let’s get to what happened in the last episode of Koffee With Karan. Actors and superstars, Rashmika Mandanna and Vijay Deverakonda, tied the knot this February after an almost decade-long relationship. In that time, they both acquired fame, wealth and were focussed on where their ambition took them. They are both at the top of their game at the moment.Then there was the wedding this year. As always when a superstar couple is on a show together for the first time after the wedding, questions about proposals come up. The answer to the proposal question by Rashmika and Vijay sent the country into full-fledged rage mode. In fact, the trolling has become so bad that the couple filed an official complaint with the Cybercrime Police, Hyderabad, regarding targeted online harassment, fabricated content, manipulated screenshots, and false break-up rumours.By now everyone knows about how this story the couple shared - albeit with hesitation. Vijay and Rashmika were at an airport after a holiday spent together, and Rashmika asked him, “why don’t we get married?” Somewhere along the conversation he joked: “Ask me 100 times and I will”. Rashmika says she asked for a whole year before the wedding in February 2025.The actress also said she’s quite open as a person and once in love, she wears her heart on her sleeves. Vijay said he’s the guy who builds barriers around him and keeps the rough exterior—even if he’s judged—because he is not someone comfortable sharing his deepest personal feelings openly.His on screen persona is somewhat still Arjun Reddy, and Vijay is not all mush openly. Rashmika is. The question is what’s so triggering about the 100 times statement that now the Hyderabad police is involved and the story is refusing to get off anyone’s timeline?Almost everyone has an opinion – and that opinion was summed up on X (formerly Twitter) as “Rashmika loves Vijay, Vijay loves Vijay” Because he came across as arrogant, narcissistic etc… depending on the degree of outrage. Social media erupted. Trolls labeled Vijay a “red flag,” claiming he was playing hard to get, while others questioned Rashmika’s dignity for pursuing him so persistently.Now the irony here is that cinema, especially Indian, have always had the hero woo the woman with songs. In fact, some of the superhit Bollywood songs are of a man wooing a woman. Mere saamne wali khidki, Dhoop mein nikla na karo roop ki rani, O Maria, Jaane jaan dhoonta phir raha, Aaaj rapat jaaye… With Rashmika and Vijay, the genders are reversed. Is that the trigger point? Or, is it the “100 times” part? Because frankly, by now, when both of them had to come up with statements (on Instagram) of a TV show conversation and the ensuing online hate, the whole matter has become quite bizarre. So, the real question is…… is it really about Rashmika-Vijay or does it say more about us?Maybe it’s about the silent rules of romance we’ve inherited; and why we get so uncomfortable when a woman rewrites them. Traditional narrative says the Bollywood hero gets to want who he wants, but the heroine only gets to be wanted.We celebrate endless movies where men refuse to take “no” for an answer, yet when a real-life woman takes the romantic initiative, she is put under a magnifying glass.Vijay came across as “arrogant” to a lot of people. But when we fall in love, don’t we fall for all kinds of people? The good, the bad, the ugly, the complicated, even the arrogant? Falling for the “bad boy” is not merely an Emily Brontë (Wuthering Heights) stereotype or a familiar cinematic trope; it happens in real life, too.We all have girlfriends who have fallen for the “bad guy”, the one with the attitude, the man who seems a little too full of himself. Or we have been those girls ourselves. Attraction has never been a neat exercise in choosing the person with the most agreeable personality, and being madly in love does not automatically mean we have lost our ability to judge character.If you watch the episode where this proposal story unfolded, what is striking is that Vijay anticipates the would-be public reaction even before answering the question. He knows how his response could come across – particularly in an age when celebrity lives are dissected under the relentless gaze of paparazzi and social media.“Karan, you won’t judge us, but people will,” he says. He may not have anticipated the extent of the backlash, or that it would become serious enough for their legal team to be involved, but he clearly understood that a private moment, once made public, could acquire a life of its own. And people did judge.Of course, a joke can sometimes reveal a deeply patriarchal attitude, even when it is delivered with a smile. But not every remark that sounds arrogant is necessarily a statement about the social order, and not every intimate exchange between a couple needs to be read as a referendum on gender equality. Context matters, as does the relationship between the people involved.Here are two people who had been in a relationship for a decade, who shared a history and a private language that the rest of us can only glimpse. To interpret one teasing remark as proof that a woman has no self-respect is to assume that we understand her relationship better than she does. And it’s deeply condescending. Which says more about us than Rashmika.The hard truth is that when a woman proposes even in the 21st century, the gesture unsettles familiar expectations because it reverses a script we have long treated as natural.But the script was never universal, and it was never simply about romance. What we are witnessing is not the collapse of a social order, but the discomfort that comes when an old convention is mistaken for an eternal truth.Confusing self-respect with love-power tussleModern women are constantly encouraged to be bold, ambitious, and independent in their careers. Yet when it comes to love, old expectations often creep back in — “know your worth,” “never to show their cards too early.”This sets up an impossible double standard. What does the modern successful woman do? Be emotionally available, but never too available? Be interested, but never appear overly invested? Be desirable, but never make the first move?Rashmika’s gesture directly challenges that outdated rulebook. Maybe that’s the point of contention.What if the man had proposed 100 times?The most telling question in this whole episode is simple: would anyone have complained if the roles were flipped? If Vijay had proposed 100 times, and then declared it on a TV show after the wedding, people would easily hail him as a dedicated romantic person. But when a woman performs that role, the commentary flips: Is she chasing him? Is she more invested than he is? Does he hold all the power in the relationship? Is she a doormat?This reaction reveals a stubborn assumption about relationships: that the person who admits their feelings first somehow loses the power struggle. But real relationships aren't business negotiations where the first person to speak loses leverage. When two people are secure and committed, who made the first move shouldn't matter at all.Calling out “bullying dressed up as feminism”As online commentary mounted, both actors stepped up to set the record straight on October 26, 2026. Rashmika released a candid statement addressing both supportive fans and angry critics. She defended her relationship and reminded people that true feminism is about freedom of choice: "Find a man who loves you so beautifully that even after you're married, you'd still want to tell him, 'Let's get married.' I would do it a thousand times – 100 is nothing. It's really that simple."She also pushed back against commentators trying to judge her private life under the guise of women's rights: "B**** about me all you want. I can take it. But talking about my family without knowing them? That's not feminism. That's bullying dressed up as feminism. Feminism was never about putting someone else down... It was always about having the freedom to choose your own life."Vijay backed her up, expressing how happy they both are. But we do not live in sane times. The trolling is still on, and a couple, who shared a personal story with trepidation - were proved to be right as to why no celebrity should ever share any personal moment – happy or sad in the future.Blunder of “epic” proportionsThe ongoing trolling is also quite ironic for a country which has women proposing to non-willing men in mythology. And these women were proposing to men who didn’t immediately say “yes”. They were persuaded. This was of course long before Hollywood made “the woman who takes charge of her romantic life” a symbol of modern independence.Rukmini wrote Krishna a letter asking him to come and carry her off. In mythology, it’s called ‘Rukmini Haran’. But the story is of Rukmini’s guts. She refused to marry the man chosen by family, and plotted her own abduction by Krishna. Then there’s Hidimba who walked up to Bhima and declared her love – despite knowing her brother Hidimb was Bhima’s enemy. Ulupi chased Arjun in exile, when he had taken a vow of celibacy, persuaded him to marry her; and then had a son with him. Savitri chose Satyavan, knowing he would die within a year.Epics are a great way to look at culture, and like in all societies, patriarchy is always a part of them. But so is a woman’s agency.And it’s not as if women’s agency has always been awarded. Remember Surpanakha? Her nose was cut off by Laxman because she dared to desire and profess her love openly. How dare she?The push and pull of what is considered acceptable and what is “offensive” has existed in mythology, in history and in modern life and love. The real asymmetry here—in the 21st century—is about who is allowed to look vulnerable without status loss.Be yourself and also be the ‘babe in the woods’A woman who chases and is turned down risks being coded as desperate, someone with no agency or worse – even a doormat. Unfortunately, all this hullabaloo makes it clear that modern women—who earn as much or more as their partners—still have to follow the regressive idea that she is a “babe in the woods” who doesn’t know her own mind when she falls in love.Also, this whole fiasco is less about raw power and more about the maintenance of a specific performance — one in which male vulnerability is essential to and female vulnerability is still suspect. articles.title: Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision again over Israel participation
articles.summary: A Dutch broadcaster reverses a decision to take part, citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation.
articles.body:
The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to take part.

The Netherlands and four other countries boycotted this year's event, after Dutch network Avrotros pulled out.

Avrotros said it would also not take part next year, but NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, stepped in and pledged last month that the country would return in 2027 .

However, NPO's media director Jurre Bosman said on Tuesday that "Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division", and NPO "has decided to forgo participation in 2027".

NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.

"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.

"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.

"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."

NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".

Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.

"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."

Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all bocotted the 2026 contest over Israel's participation, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Eurovision organisers have announced a number of changes in an attempt to address the divisions, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition, and changes to the voting.

As well as the Netherlands, Ireland will also not take part in 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.

The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.

Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year with the dance track Bangaranga.

articles.title: Arrest warrant for dad of A66 teen over funeral assault
articles.summary: Gye Worthy fails to appear in court after attacking a celebrant at the funeral of his son.
articles.body:
An arrest warrant has been issued for a man who attacked a celebrant at the funeral of his son, one of five men and two police officers killed in a head-on crash.

Gye Worthy, 40, admitted common assault and resisting arrest at his son's funeral at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough after a disturbance during the service on 9 September.

His son Cole Worthy, 17, died when the Volkswagen Passat he and four others were in collided with a marked armed police car on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of 22 August.

On Tuesday Worthy failed to turn up for sentencing at Teesside Crown Court, which heard he had not spoken to his solicitors or explained his absence to the court.

Worthy, of Ruskin Avenue, Middlesbrough, was also due to be sentenced for stealing four bottles of wine worth £30 from a shop on 8 October.

Deputy District Judge Julia Baggs agreed to an application by the prosecution for a warrant to be issued, "not backed by bail".

That meant he would have to be held in custody ahead of a future court date once he has been located.

The deputy district judge said: "In these circumstances, I do accept the application for a warrant not backed by bail."

Worthy previously admitted assaulting the celebrant Paul Maull during the funeral service for Cole Worthy.

Cole Worthy's funeral was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.

PC Blades had been travelling along the A66 with his colleague PC Tom Clough when their car was struck head-on by the Passat travelling in the wrong direction.

The pair were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered a camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit which preceded the crash, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The others killed in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-old Theo Rae.

It later emerged a property on a street in Acklam, Middlesbrough, linked to the Worthy family had been rammed by a car shortly before the fatal crash.

articles.title: The AI social paradox: Better at communicating, worse at connecting?
articles.summary: A text from a family member. An email from the boss. A friend seeking advice after an argument.
articles.body: A text from a family member. An email from the boss. A friend seeking advice after an argument. These are ordinary moments that are part of everyday interactions. Yet, increasingly, there is another participant in these conversations, one that neither feels emotions nor has any personal stake in the relationship - artificial intelligence.For generations, people learnt social etiquette, understood different perspectives and navigated relationships through actual interactions. They often said the wrong things, misunderstood intentions and learnt from those experiences.Now, with AI offering an instant answer to every social dilemma, some of that effort can be outsourced.So, why has replying to an ordinary message become something we might need assistance with? Also while AI may make us more articulate, polite and confident, does that necessarily make us better at connecting?A 'social animal' with AI?Humans have long been described as social animals. Relationships are shaped not merely by what one says, but by how they listen, react, disagree and adapt to one another.AI, however, offers something human relationships rarely can: immediate attention, endless patience and responses tailored to specific concerns. There is no awkward silence, no raised eyebrow and seemingly no fear of embarrassment.This was highlighted by Shailesh K Nevatia, founder director of Grandeavour Communication, having spent nearly 25 years in the communication industry but described himself as shy when it comes to open communication concerning himself.He said AI helps him navigate differences of opinion, offering perspectives he might otherwise overlook. "With humans we may have certain opinions, views, or thoughts, while with AI, the most valuable thing it offers is not the right answer but a different perspective than us," he said.Nevertheless, he maintained that the emotional depth, vulnerability and shared experiences of human relationships cannot be replicated by a chatbot.When the robot does the talkingThe concern with AI-assisted communication is not just that people are using it to find the right words, but that repeated reliance on it could weaken their confidence in finding those words themselves.For instance, Riddhi turns to ChatGPT almost instinctively when responding at times. Whether she needs to sound polite yet firm in a professional email or find a way to decline plans with friends, AI helps her navigate the interaction. "It's not like I can't reply without AI, but having someone to proofread the convos is better than just listening to how they sound in my head," she said.Yet, the reassurance comes with a trade-off for her. "AI has such a grasp on my writing that I am not very confident even while writing this, and that is, without being said, one of the biggest disadvantages." She also called to embrace AI but be careful.Now that AI has become a new normal, its not possible to go back to the non-AI era, but its also important to not let it become the master of ourselves.Her experience pointed to a potential paradox: a tool intended to make communication easier can also leave users less confident about communicating independently.The stakes may be higher when AI is used not just to frame a response, but to interpret another person's intentions. Consider someone who turns to a chatbot after an argument and asks who was at fault. The response can sound considered and convincing, but it is based on the account presented to the system, which may omit details or reflect the user's own biases.In that context, Reshmithaa Nair, counselling psychologist at SPARSH Hospital, Hennur Road, warned that such interactions can reinforce confirmation bias, making people more convinced of their existing interpretation rather than open to another perspective.That matters because disagreements are also opportunities to develop social skills. Understanding another person's point of view, managing uncomfortable emotions and responding to unexpected reactions require practice, not simply a well-worded reply."Social skills are learned in actual situations that involve emotions, misunderstanding, conflict, and sometimes rejection," Nair further explained.Repeatedly delegating these situations to AI could reduce opportunities to develop empathy, emotional intelligence and the ability to navigate uncertainty. A person may learn to phrase a difficult message more effectively without necessarily becoming better at handling the conversation that follows.The missing human touchA message is not simply a collection of sentences. Its meaning can change with the relationship between the people involved, their shared experiences and even the pauses between words.Ritu Mehrotra, Founder and CEO of Shunya Labs, a voice AI company, pointed out that natural communication involves much more than language."Communication is not only about words, it’s also about tone, pauses, context, emotion and all the things we communicate without explicitly saying them."Advances in voice AI are making it possible for technology to interpret language, intent and context with greater sophistication, including across different accents and communication styles. Yet, recognising emotional signals is not the same as experiencing emotions."And as AI is becoming a part of more and more personal conversations, we have to realise that understanding emotion is not feeling it. Trust, privacy, and transparency must be fundamental," she said.AI should help people connect with one another, not replicate human empathy or replace human relationships.A chatbot may recognise expressions of sadness or affection and produce an empathetic-sounding response. But recognising emotional patterns is different from sharing the emotional responsibility of a human relationship. For ex, an AI chatbot was asked to give advice to reply on a (hypothetical) "text to a friend who was laid off"While the response was considerate, it was also generic. It offered comfort without knowing the friend's emotional state, personality or the nature of the relationship. Even a seemingly caring question like “Are you OK?” may fall flat when the person is looking for encouragement rather than a question whose answer seems obvious. A more personal response might acknowledge the setback while affirming the friend's abilities: “OMG, that's awful. I know the job market is tough, but you're talented. You'll land on your feet.”The difference is not simply about choosing warmer words. It is about understanding what a particular person might need in that moment, something a chatbot may struggle to judge without sufficient context.There is also the question of authenticity. When a message is carefully constructed by AI, it may communicate the intended information effectively. But does it still sound like the person sending it?In this example, of AI removing the human touch, another chatbot was asked "Someone close to me is grieving. I don't know what to say, and I'm afraid of making things worse. What should I tell them?". It gave a response, which is not wrong but is too robotic. "I am here with you. I care about your pain. Speak if you wish; silence is acceptable." Perfect words but not someone who is comforting says in such "rigid tone"The little hesitations, imperfect expressions and familiar phrases that characterise someone's communication can disappear beneath polished language. A message can become more grammatically correct while feeling less personal.Not all badDismissing AI as a threat to social skills, however, would overlook how it can help people who struggle to express themselves.For Pooja, a college student who hesitates to speak up in front of the entire class or repeatedly ask friends to explain something, AI offers a space where she can ask questions without worrying about others' reactions.She uses it to understand complicated topics and brainstorm ideas, sometimes asking ChatGPT to explain something as though she were a 10-year-old.What I love most is that I can ask the dumbest questions without feeling embarrassed. But I also feel it's very easy to become too dependent on it.Yet, she recognises the possibility of becoming overly reliant on it. "AI can give you answers in seconds, but actually understanding and learning something is still on us."For others, AI serves as a sounding board before difficult conversations. It can also help people become more mindful of how their words might affect others. It can suggest more inclusive language, flag potentially insensitive phrasing and help users consider perspectives they might otherwise overlook. For someone unsure how to communicate across differences, this can offer a starting point for more thoughtful interactions.But knowing which words are considered appropriate is not necessarily the same as understanding why they matter. Genuine inclusivity requires empathy and a willingness to understand experiences different from one's own, qualities that must extend beyond the words suggested by a chatbot.Also, in such cases, might not give you the perfect answer, but may help you think in the right direction and give you options that you may not have thought about. In another hypothetical test, a chatbot was asked how to support a family member struggling with their mental health without pushing them away. While its response was not fully correct, it offered different approaches to consider, giving the person a starting point for thinking about how to respond.Thus, the value, then, may not lie in AI providing the perfect answer, but in helping someone see possibilities they had not considered. The important distinction is whether people use these suggestions to develop their own judgement or simply follow them without question.As Shruti Rajan Kappil, clinical lead, excellence and quality at a mental health care platform Amaha, explained, that while the need to feel heard and supported is fundamental to human relationships, not every concern feels safe to share. Shame, embarrassment and fear of judgement often prevent people from opening up, particularly where stigma remains prevalent.AI offers an alternative, but Kappil pointed to an important distinction. "Good support often needs honest disagreement or gentle challenge with a different point of view. AI tends to be agreeable more often than not, and being agreed with is easily mistaken for being helped."She also noted that repeatedly seeking AI's approval before sending a message can become a form of reassurance seeking. While it offers immediate relief, constantly checking whether one's words are "correct" may gradually undermine confidence in one's own judgement.Shristi Chaudhari, senior executive, regulatory intelligence and market research at Bureau Veritas, uses AI almost daily to condense regulatory updates. Increasingly, she also turns to it for interpersonal communication.From identifying emotional undertones to making messages warmer and more polite for colleagues and professional contacts, AI has become a useful sounding board.While AI can refine written communication, help us anticipate reactions and interpret conversational nuances, it cannot replace the soft skills, verbal cues and lived experiences that shape genuine human connections.These experiences suggest AI can help people prepare for conversations, overcome language barriers and articulate thoughts they might otherwise struggle to express.Perfect talks, weaker bonds?Communication is one of the ways human beings establish connection. But effective communication and meaningful connection are not necessarily the same thing.One involves expressing something clearly. The other requires understanding, trust, emotional involvement and vulnerability.Tanvi Mankodi, assistant professor at SPJIMR, believes the deeper concern is not whether AI will replace human relationships, but what excessive dependence might do to our ability to participate in them."For me, the essence of human relationships is about our vulnerabilities, about our imperfections, and about how we try to relate with each other with our discomforts and uncertainties," she said.Misunderstandings, difficult conversations and moments when people struggle to find the right words are also experiences through which patience, compassion and empathy develop."Rather than worrying about AI replacing human relations, I am more worried about how if we use AI in a way that we are dependent on it, it might reduce our ability to be vulnerable and to be human," she added.Her concern captures the paradox: in trying to eliminate the discomfort of human interaction, we may also remove experiences that make relationships meaningful.Of course, not every AI-generated message weakens a relationship, and the long-term effects of outsourcing everyday communication are still being understood. AI may help some people overcome barriers to social participation while encouraging others to avoid interactions through which confidence develops. But, the concern is can it address the individuality and complexity of human behaviour?However, using AI to prepare for a difficult discussion is one thing. Allowing it to decide how we interpret another person's intentions and what we say in every interaction is another.The point is not whether AI can offer thoughtful, nuanced or well-structured answers to human dilemmas. It is whether those answers can replicate the emotional understanding, vulnerability and lived experiences through which we learn to navigate relationships and grow socially. After all, relationships are not assignments to be completed with perfectly structured answers. They evolve through disagreement, compromise and sometimes saying something imperfectly but sincerely.Perhaps the real challenge is not learning how to communicate better with AI, but ensuring that, in the process, we do not forget how to connect without it.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: South Sudan cattle raids: Co-oridanted attacks kill at least 72 people in Warrup state
articles.summary: The cycle of revenge attacks continue as the country heads towards its first  election since independence.
articles.body:
At least 72 people have been killed during cattle raids in South Sudan's northern Warrap state, according to the regional government.

An unspecified number of cattle were taken and homes burnt during what was a "co-ordinated attack" on Monday involving two communities in Tonj North county, the state authorities said.

Such deadly violence is often part of a cycle of revenge attacks as cattle are a main source of wealth and pride for many communities and are also important as young men need them as dowries to get married.

Clashes over territory are also common across the country as it prepares to hold its first election since its independence in 2011 - delayed because of a brutal civil war.

The clashes occurred near the border of Warrap and Unity states in the area of Akop Payam, with some members from Lou Ariik community said to have attacked those from Apuk Padoch community.

William Wol Mayom Bol, Warrap state's information minister, said they followed deadly violence last Friday that claimed eight lives.

The state governor, Angelo Ngot Mayar, sent his condolences to bereaved families and directed security agencies to evacuate the wounded.

He said efforts were under way recover the cattle and find those behind the assault.

The state has also appealed to humanitarian partners to support vulnerable women, children and elderly left without food, shelter and medicine.

In August, at least 60 people were killed and 50 injured in an attack in the same area of Warrap state, according to Acled, the non-profit conflict monitoring group.

A similar attack in March led to 58 deaths and 71 injuries.

Last year, a six-month state of emergency was declared in Warrup in efforts to quell the increasing violence.

The UN has also voiced its concerns about the situation in South Sudan as the world's youngest country heads towards presidential elections due to be held in December .

The poll was initially delayed by the civil war, which ended in 2018 with a fragile peace deal signed between President Salva Kiir and his deputy Riek Machar.

However tensions between the leaders led to further delays: Machar was sacked as vice-president and arrested earlier last year and charged with murder, treason and crimes against humanity, which he denies.

He has been under house arrest in the capital, Juba, since March last year as fighting persists in some areas of the country.

Preparations for the elections have lagged and human rights groups have raised questions over whether the country can complete key things like voter registration and security arrangements before the vote.

articles.title: In 2025, James Comey was indicted over congressional testimony before a judge dismissed the case; in 2026, a social-media threat indictment followed, and he now faces a third federal prosecution
articles.summary: The US Justice Department has made a third attempt to bring criminal charges against former FBI director James Comey, this time over allegations that he
articles.body: The US Justice Department has made a third attempt to bring criminal charges against former FBI director James Comey, this time over allegations that he disclosed national defence information to an unauthorised person in 2016, according to court records.Prosecutors have filed a criminal information accusing Comey of two counts of violating the Espionage Act by allegedly transmitting national defence information to someone not authorised to receive it. The filing, made under seal earlier this month, was unsealed on Monday at the request of Comey's legal team.The latest move does not amount to a grand jury indictment or a criminal complaint. Instead, prosecutors used criminal information, a formal charging document filed directly by the government, to preserve the case before the statute of limitations expires. The Justice Department has said the procedure is recognised in federal courts.The allegations stem from a 2016 New York Times report about Yahoo's role in US email surveillance. According to court filings, the department alleges that Comey directed staff to speak with a Times reporter about the accuracy of an earlier Reuters report.Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said the former FBI director maintains his innocence and that the allegations concern a matter investigated twice during the first Trump administration, with prosecutors deciding on both occasions not to bring charges.In a video statement posted on Monday, Comey said the latest action was an “appalling abuse” of the Justice Department. He added that he remained innocent and was not afraid of those seeking to prosecute him.The latest effort comes amid Comey's long-running feud with President Donald Trump, who fired him during his first term and has repeatedly called for his prosecution.Why the latest filing is differentThe criminal information was filed in early October, shortly before the 10-year statute of limitations for the alleged offence was due to expire. Comey's lawyers have challenged the move, arguing that filing the document cannot extend the deadline applicable to an indictment.The legal team has also sought to have the case dismissed. During an emergency hearing, prosecutors agreed to refrain from seeking an indictment for 30 days, according to court filings.US District Judge Trevor McFadden ordered the documents unsealed on Monday, citing the public interest in criminal charges involving a former FBI director. The judge did not rule on the merits of the allegations.Former prosecutors and defence lawyers told CBS News that using a criminal information in this manner was highly unusual. Some argued that the filing appeared designed to keep the case alive despite the approaching deadline.The Justice Department has defended the procedure, saying that filing a criminal information to pause the statute of limitations is a recognised practice that has been approved by multiple federal appeals courts.Two previous cases against ComeyThe latest action follows two earlier attempts to prosecute Comey.In September 2025, a federal grand jury indicted him on charges of lying to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding. The allegations centred on his testimony about whether he had authorised an FBI employee to act as an anonymous source. A judge dismissed the case in November 2025, ruling that the prosecutor who brought it had been improperly appointed.In April 2026, Comey was indicted in North Carolina over a social media post featuring seashells arranged to form the numbers “86 47”. Prosecutors alleged that the image constituted a threat against Trump, the 47th US president. Comey denied wrongdoing, saying he did not know the significance attributed to the numbers. That case remains pending.Comey's lawyers have argued that the prosecutions are politically motivated and have sought to dismiss the North Carolina case on grounds including vindictive and selective prosecution.The former FBI director's clashes with Trump date back to 2017, when the president fired him amid the FBI investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 US presidential election. Comey's firing led to the appointment of special counsel Robert Mueller, whose investigation continued through much of Trump's first term.The latest case also comes as a federal judge ruled on Monday that the administration had unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor in New York. The judge ordered her reinstatement and back pay after she challenged her dismissal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body:
Toppled trees have forced the postponement of a match in Scottish football's fifth tier on player and spectator safety grounds.

Newton Stewart were scheduled to host Gretna 2008 at Blairmount Park in the Lowland League West but the club posted pictures of the scale of the problem being faced.

One tree had caused significant damage to a perimeter fence and was lying over the pitch.

The club said it was being removed but it needed to get a professional assessment of other trees nearby with high winds expected throughout the day.

The area around the ground has seen "significant damage" in the past few days due to storms sweeping across the country.

The club warned anyone heading up to the area that it might be unsafe until a proper assessment was carried out.

At the weekend fallen trees blocked the entrance to the ground and now more have come down next to the pitch.

The one overhanging the pitch has been removed but further assessment will be carried out by experts to see if there is a risk of further damage.

articles.title: Teenager from England starts a 3D printing business at 15 to make skyscraper models and now earns £17,000 a year shipping orders overseas
articles.summary: A teenage 3D printing business that began with skyscraper models has grown into a small enterprise earning about £17,000 a year.
articles.body: A teenage 3D printing business that began with skyscraper models has grown into a small enterprise earning about £17,000 a year. Reece, a 17-year-old from Worksop in Nottinghamshire, launched the venture at 15, and today his products reach customers across the United Kingdom and overseas. He now runs four printers at home, day and night, to keep up with orders, and his promotional work has made him well known locally. For a teenager who is still in education, that makes the enterprise remarkably well established, turning a personal passion into paid work with real customers and a varied product range.A printer from his family and a love of skyscrapers set the business in motion at 15Reece told the BBC that his family gave him a printer to support his love of model skyscrapers, an interest he has had for a few years. His idea was simple, print models of tall buildings so that he could compare their sizes. His favourite buildings are the Burj Khalifa and The Shard.Selling came soon after. He began to sell his work so that he could afford better printing equipment. As sales grew, he started to move away from skyscrapers to concentrate on improving his 3D printing skills.Hearing aid accessories and communication tools for non-verbal children widen the product rangeReece now makes a wide variety of products, including items that support people with health issues and disabilities. Hearing aid accessories and communication tools for non-verbal children are among them. He says he wants to help others because he knows what it is like.Some of his orders have been shipped as far as Chicago.Talking to customers and promoting his work online has boosted his confidence and communicationReece told the BBC that he struggled to make friends when he was younger because of his autism, which can make social interaction and communication difficult. He also has epilepsy, and he said his struggles once left him feeling that he was not important.Running the business has pushed him in the opposite direction. Speaking to customers and promoting his products on social media have, in his view, made him happier and more talkative. They have also taught him something he once found hard to grasp. “I understand banter now,” he said, adding that he has made it a routine and thinks he might understand sarcasm in a few years if he keeps going.His father went from building the printers to running postage and packaging as sales grewReece’s father, Thomas, told the same broadcaster that when the business started he was head of construction, building the printers, before being demoted to head of postage and packaging. He said Reece found his first social media video difficult and had to practise repeatedly before he felt comfortable in front of the camera. He joked that his son now thinks he is a celebrity.Thomas said that after all the challenges his son has faced, including operations, Reece has come through smiling. He added that he simply wants his son to be happy and healthy, and that he is very proud of him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Lilly Jones was found in woodlands in south Wales, two days after she had been reported missing.
articles.body:
A 14-year-old boy has denied murdering a teenage girl whose body was found in woodland.

Lilly Jones, also 14, was discovered in Duffryn Park in Blaina, Blaenau Gwent, on 22 June, two days after her family reported her missing.

At Newport Crown Court on Tuesday, the defendant from Blaenau Gwent, who cannot be named for legal reasons, pleaded not guilty to her murder.

Dressed in a white shirt and a dark coloured tie, he sat in the dock flanked by four security officers.

When he was asked by the clerk if he pleaded guilty or not guilty to the charge of murder, he replied quietly, "not guilty".

The families of both Lilly and the defendant were in court for the hearing.

Lilly was previously described as "the most beautiful, kind and caring little girl" , who was "completely and utterly herself".

articles.title: Dinosaur skeleton goes to auction in New York with £4.5m price tag
articles.summary: The auction of the rare skeleton comes amid debate in the scientific community about whether dinosaur remains should end up in private hands or public view.
articles.body:
The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex is up for auction - with a price-tag of at least $6m (£4.5m).

Nicknamed "Jodi", the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton will be auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.

The Late Cretaceous carnivore is expected to fetch up to $9m when it goes under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed "Gus", for a record $50.1m (£37.4m) in July.

The sales comes as some in the scientific community debate whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately.

Sotheby's described "Jodi" as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".

The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science." The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.

Megan Jenkins, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".

"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jenkins said.

Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.

"Jodi" was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.

The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hall Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.

Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from "Jodi" in 2006.

The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.

The auction of "Jodi" comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.

Researchers told the BBC after the sale of "Gus" that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.

Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".

"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."

He said that the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.

Responding to today's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that "Jodi" could disappear from public view.

"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.

But Jenkins told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.

"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

articles.title: Rothbury Estate appeal nears target following government pledge
articles.summary: The government pledges £1.9m to wildlife groups' efforts to buy the Rothbury Estate.
articles.body:
Conservation groups aiming to raise £30m to buy a vast upland estate are within touching distance of their target following a £1.9m government pledge.

The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust are looking to acquire the 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate in its entirety as part of plans boost wildlife, restore bogs and promote nature-friendly farming.

Their fundraising efforts - now standing at £29m thanks to the latest donation - have attracted backing from the likes of Sir David Attenborough with the window for public donations running until the end of this week.

However, some members of the Northumberland farming community said they viewed the project as "a folly".

The wildlife groups previously purchased part of the estate, including the Simonside Hills, from the Duke of Northumberland's son, Lord Max Percy, in 2024.

If successful in buying the remainder, the organisations claim there is the potential to develop a "40-mile nature recovery corridor stretching from the North East coast to Kielder on the central Scottish border".

It could also see a reduction in the number of sheep from 1,500 to 500 with the number of cattle quadrupled to 200.

The government grant was announced on Monday at the UN Global Biodiversity Conference, COP17, taking place in Armenia.

Craig Bennett OBE, chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the funding would "take us another step closer to realising our vision for one of the largest nature recovery projects England has ever seen".

He added it was a "stamp of approval" for the project on the back of "millions generously donated by philanthropists, charitable funds and thousands of members of the public".

Earlier this year, though, tenant farmer Chris Armstrong, who oversees 1,000 acres (405 hectares) close to the site, warned local opinion was split .

He told the BBC: "I would put it very much akin to the Brexit vote. I would think it would be that finely split.

"I think the majority of the farming community see this as a folly."
